<reason>PRO (Side B) built the cleaner path: the existence of shrinkflation as a strategy is itself proof that current gram/unit-price disclosure fails at the point of decision, and CON's own [A2.2] admission that firms shrink "to preserve price points consumers anchor on" handed B that inference. B then answered A's memory objection directly (the sticker is actively read and compared against the rival beside it; the grams are not), and treated the baseline/mixed-delta problems as ordinary drafting (previous regular size, show two lines, safe harbour) rather than fatal flaws. CON fought well — the product-vs-store churn distinction, the "what is the 'was'" baseline point, and the "every fix grows the regime" framing were sharp and forced B to elaborate — but A's core "the information already exists" premise never recovered from the anchoring concession, and the "different proposal" closing overstated modest implementation details as a motion swap. A also carried slightly more clipping costs and its A2 answer blurred B's actual Q2 until the closing. Competitive, but B made the decision easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 ([B2.1]-[B2.3]) pitting A's "plain ink already discloses everything" against A's own "wallpaper" fear, then arguing that shrinkflation exists only because the gram count isn't read — reinforced in Rebuttal 2 by turning A's anchoring admission into the case's central proof.</best_rebuttal>
